title: Collecting Data
content:
# Collecting Data

## Learning Objectives
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
- Distinguish between primary and secondary data
- Understand different sampling methods and their advantages
- Recognise bias in data collection
- Design a simple questionnaire
- Evaluate the reliability and validity of data sources

## Introduction

Before we can analyse data, we need to collect it. The way data is collected has a huge impact on the conclusions we can draw. A poorly designed survey or a biased sample can lead to misleading results.

For example, if a school wants to know whether students prefer the new lunch menu, asking only students in the dinner queue would give biased results -- students who dislike the menu may have stopped buying school lunches altogether.

---

## Key Concepts

### Primary vs Secondary Data

**Primary data** is data you collect yourself for a specific purpose.

- Surveys and questionnaires
- Experiments and observations
- Interviews
- Measurements you take

**Advantages:** Collected for your specific purpose; you know how it was collected; up to date.

**Disadvantages:** Time-consuming; expensive; limited sample size.

---

**Secondary data** is data that has already been collected by someone else.

- Government statistics (e.g. census data)
- Newspapers and websites
- Published research
- Company records

**Advantages:** Quick and cheap to obtain; often large datasets; can cover wide areas.

**Disadvantages:** May not match your exact needs; could be out of date; you don't know how it was collected.

---

### Population and Samples

The **population** is the entire group you are interested in studying.

A **sample** is a smaller subset of the population that is actually studied.

> In most real-world situations, it is impractical or impossible to survey the entire population, so we take a sample and use it to draw conclusions about the population.

For a sample to be useful, it must be **representative** of the population -- it should reflect the characteristics of the whole group.

The **sample size** is the number of items in the sample. Larger samples tend to be more representative, but take more time and money to collect.

---

### Sampling Methods

#### Random Sampling

**Random sampling** means every member of the population has an **equal chance** of being selected.

**Method:** Assign each member a number, then use a random number generator or draw numbers from a hat.

**Advantage:** Avoids bias; every member has a fair chance.

**Disadvantage:** May not be representative if the sample is small; needs a complete list of the population.

---

#### Systematic Sampling

**Systematic sampling** selects members at regular intervals from an ordered list.

**Method:** Choose every $k$th item, where:

$$k = \frac{\text{population size}}{\text{sample size}}$$

**Example:** To select 20 students from a school of 400, choose every $\frac{400}{20} = 20\text{th}$ student from an alphabetical list.

**Advantage:** Simple and quick to carry out.

**Disadvantage:** Can be biased if there is a hidden pattern in the list.

---

#### Stratified Sampling

**Stratified sampling** divides the population into groups (strata) and selects from each group in proportion to its size.

**Formula for the number to select from each stratum:**

$$\text{Number from stratum} = \frac{\text{stratum size}}{\text{population size}} \times \text{sample size}$$

**Example:** A school has 600 students in Year 10 and 400 students in Year 11. To take a stratified sample of 50 students:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Year 10: } &\frac{600}{1000} \times 50 = 30 \text{ students} \\
\text{Year 11: } &\frac{400}{1000} \times 50 = 20 \text{ students}
\end{aligned}$$

**Advantage:** Ensures each group is proportionally represented.

**Disadvantage:** Requires knowledge of the population structure.

---

### Bias

**Bias** occurs when certain outcomes or responses are systematically favoured over others, making the results unrepresentative.

**Common sources of bias:**
- **Leading questions** that push respondents toward a particular answer
- **Non-representative samples** (e.g. surveying only one age group)
- **Voluntary response** (people who feel strongly are more likely to respond)
- **Time of day** or **location** of data collection

---

## Worked Examples

### Example 1

**Question:** A factory has 300 workers: 180 in production, 80 in administration, and 40 in management. A stratified sample of 50 workers is to be taken. How many from each department should be selected?

**Solution:**

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Production: } &\frac{180}{300} \times 50 = 30 \\
\text{Administration: } &\frac{80}{300} \times 50 = 13.\overline{3} \approx 13 \\
\text{Management: } &\frac{40}{300} \times 50 = 6.\overline{6} \approx 7
\end{aligned}$$

**Answer:** 30 from production, 13 from administration, and 7 from management.

> **Note:** When rounding, check the total still adds to 50. Here $30 + 13 + 7 = 50$. ✓

---

### Example 2

**Question:** A student wants to find out if people in her town support a new bypass. She stands outside the local supermarket on a Monday morning and asks 30 people. Give two reasons why this sample may be biased.

**Solution:**

1. **Time bias:** On a Monday morning, the sample will over-represent people who do not work during the day (e.g. retired people, shift workers) and under-represent full-time workers.

2. **Location bias:** Only people who shop at that supermarket are included. People who shop elsewhere or who don't visit that area are excluded.

---

### Example 3

**Question:** Criticise this survey question: "Don't you agree that the school should build a new sports hall?"

**Solution:**

This is a **leading question** because it starts with "Don't you agree" which pushes the respondent toward saying yes. A better question would be:

"Do you think the school should build a new sports hall?" with response options: Yes / No / No opinion.

---

### Example 4

**Question:** There are 1200 students in a school. The headteacher wants a systematic sample of 60. Describe how to select this sample.

**Solution:**

Step 1: Calculate the sampling interval:
$$k = \frac{1200}{60} = 20$$

Step 2: List all 1200 students (e.g. alphabetically or by student number).

Step 3: Choose a random starting point between 1 and 20, say the $7\text{th}$ student.

Step 4: Select every $20\text{th}$ student: the $7\text{th}$, $27\text{th}$, $47\text{th}$, $67\text{th}$, ... until 60 students are selected.

---

## Common Mistakes

| Mistake | Why It's Wrong | Correct Approach |
|---------|---------------|------------------|
| Thinking a large sample removes all bias | A large biased sample is still biased | Focus on HOW the sample is selected, not just its size |
| Using "Do you agree..." in questionnaires | This is a leading question | Use neutral phrasing with balanced options |
| Forgetting to round stratified sample sizes | You can't survey 13.3 people | Round appropriately and check the total matches |
| Confusing population with sample | The population is everyone; the sample is who you actually study | Clearly define both before collecting data |
| Assuming secondary data is always reliable | It may be outdated, biased, or collected differently | Always check the source, date, and method |

---

## Practice Questions

### Foundation Tier

1. State whether each of the following is primary or secondary data:
   (a) Measuring the heights of students in your class
   (b) Using census data from the government website
   (c) Counting the number of cars in the school car park

2. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of primary data.

3. A student wants to survey people about a new park. He asks his 10 friends. Give two reasons why this is not a good sample.

4. Rewrite this biased question: "Surely you think homework is a waste of time?"

5. A school has 500 students. A random sample of 25 is needed. Describe how to take a random sample.

6. Explain the difference between a population and a sample.

### Higher Tier

7. A company has 240 men and 160 women. A stratified sample of 40 is needed. How many men and how many women should be selected?

8. A gym has members in three age groups: Under 30 (450), 30-50 (350), Over 50 (200). A stratified sample of 100 is to be taken. Calculate the number from each group.

9. Describe how to take a systematic sample of 30 from a population of 900.

10. Explain why a voluntary online survey about a political issue is likely to produce biased results.

11. A council wants to survey residents about a new recycling scheme. Compare the advantages and disadvantages of using a postal questionnaire versus face-to-face interviews.

12. Give one advantage and one disadvantage of stratified sampling compared to random sampling.

---

## Answers

1. (a) Primary (b) Secondary (c) Primary

2. Advantage: collected for your specific purpose so it's relevant. Disadvantage: time-consuming and expensive to collect.

3. (i) Only 10 people is too small a sample to represent the whole population. (ii) Asking only friends means the sample is not representative -- they may share similar views.

4. "How do you feel about homework?" with options such as: Very useful / Useful / Not useful / A waste of time.

5. Assign each student a number from 1 to 500. Use a random number generator to produce 25 different numbers between 1 and 500. Select the students with those numbers.

6. The population is the entire group being studied. A sample is a smaller subset of the population that is actually surveyed or measured.

7. Men: $\frac{240}{400} \times 40 = 24$. Women: $\frac{160}{400} \times 40 = 16$.

8. Under 30: $\frac{450}{1000} \times 100 = 45$. 30--50: $\frac{350}{1000} \times 100 = 35$. Over 50: $\frac{200}{1000} \times 100 = 20$.

9. Calculate $k = \frac{900}{30} = 30$. Number the population 1 to 900. Choose a random start between 1 and 30 (e.g. 14). Select every 30th: 14, 44, 74, 104, ...

10. Only people who feel strongly about the issue are likely to respond (voluntary response bias), so moderate views will be under-represented. Also, only people with internet access can respond.

11. Postal: cheaper, wider reach, but low response rate and no way to clarify questions. Face-to-face: higher response rate, can explain questions, but expensive, time-consuming, and interviewer bias possible.

12. Advantage: stratified sampling guarantees proportional representation of subgroups. Disadvantage: requires prior knowledge of the population structure (sizes of each stratum).

---

## Exam Tips

- When asked to criticise a sampling method, focus on **who is excluded** and **why the sample might not represent the population**.
- For stratified sampling calculations, always show the fraction multiplied by the sample size, and check your answers sum to the correct total.
- When designing questionnaires, avoid leading questions, provide response boxes, and include a time frame ("In the last month...").

---

## Summary

- **Primary data** is collected first-hand; **secondary data** is pre-existing
- A **sample** is a subset of the **population** and should be representative
- **Random sampling** gives everyone an equal chance of selection
- **Systematic sampling** selects every $k$th item from an ordered list
- **Stratified sampling** selects proportionally from subgroups: $\frac{\text{stratum}}{\text{population}} \times \text{sample size}$
- **Bias** makes results unrepresentative and can arise from leading questions, non-random samples, or poor timing/location
